questions.stem:
The cities Lucknow (L), Jaipur (J) and Delhi (D) are represented in the following diagram. Lucknow lies $500\text{ km}$ directly east of Jaipur, and $\text{J}\hat{\text{L}}\text{D} = 25^\circ$.

**diagram not to scale**

![Triangle JDL with J at the left end of a 500 km horizontal side JL, a North arrow at J, D above, and angle 25° at L.](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q1.png)

The bearing of D from J is $034^\circ$.

parts.label: a
parts.markscheme:
Let N be North

$\text{N}\hat{\text{J}}\text{D} = 34^\circ$ OR $\text{D}\hat{\text{J}}\text{L} = 56^\circ$ (must be labelled or indicated in diagram): ***(A1)***

$\text{J}\hat{\text{D}}\text{L} = 99\ (^\circ)$ ***A1***

> **Note:** Accept $\dfrac{11\pi}{20}$, $1.73$ (radians).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance between Lucknow and Delhi.
parts.markscheme:
attempt to apply the sine rule ***(M1)***

$\dfrac{\text{DL}}{\sin 56^\circ} = \dfrac{500}{\sin 99^\circ}$ OR $\dfrac{\text{DL}}{\sin 0.977384\ldots} = \dfrac{500}{\sin 1.72787\ldots}$ ***(A1)***

$419.685\ldots$

$\text{DL} = 420$ (km) ***A1***

> **Note:** Award ***M1A1A0*** for $261$ (km) from use of degrees with GDC set in radians (with or without working).

questions.stem: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x) = 2x - x^3$ and $g(x) = \tan x$.

parts.label: a
parts.markscheme:
attempt to substitute $g$ into $f$ ***(M1)***

$(f \circ g)(x) = 2\tan x - \tan^3 x$ ***A1***

parts.label: b
parts.text:
On the following grid, sketch the graph of $y = (f \circ g)(x)$ for $-1 \leq x \leq 1$. Write down and clearly label the coordinates of any local maximum or minimum points.

![Empty grid with x from −1 to 1 and y from −2 to 2.](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q3-grid.png)
parts.markscheme:
![Graph of y = 2 tan x − tan³ x for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1: through the origin, minimum (−0.685, −1.09), maximum (0.685, 1.09).](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q3b-ms.png)

***A1A1A1***

> **Note:** ***A1*** for approximately correct odd function passing through the origin with a maximum above $y = 1$ and a minimum below $y = -1$.  
> ***A1*** for endpoints at $x = \pm 1$ and $y$ in the intervals $[0.6,\ 0.8]$ and $[-0.8,\ -0.6]$.  
> ***A1*** for maximum in approximately correct position and labelled $(0.685,\ 1.09)$ AND minimum in approximately correct position and labelled $(-0.685,\ -1.09)$. For approximate position, allow $-0.8 \leq x \leq -0.6$, $-1.2 \leq y \leq -1$ for minimum and $0.6 \leq x \leq 0.8$, $1 \leq y \leq 1.2$ for maximum. If the candidate gives the coordinates of extrema below their sketch, only award this mark if extrema are marked in the correct interval (eg by a dot).

questions.stem: The total number of children, $y$, visiting a park depends on the highest temperature, $T$, in degrees Celsius ($^\circ$C). A park official predicts the total number of children visiting his park on any given day using the model $y = -0.6T^2 + 23T + 110$, where $10 \leq T \leq 35$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use this model to estimate the number of children in the park on a day when the highest temperature is $25^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.label: b
parts.intro:
An ice cream vendor investigates the relationship between the total number of children visiting the park and the number of ice creams sold, $x$. The following table shows the data collected on five different days.

| **Total number of children** $(y)$ | $81$ | $175$ | $202$ | $346$ | $360$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Ice creams sold** $(x)$ | $15$ | $27$ | $23$ | $35$ | $46$ |
parts.text: Find an appropriate regression equation that will allow the vendor to predict the number of ice creams sold on a day when there are $y$ children in the park.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence, use your regression equation to predict the number of ice creams that the vendor sells on a day when the highest temperature is $25^\circ\text{C}$.
parts.markscheme:
attempt to substitute their answer to part (a) into their regression equation for either $x$ or $y$ ***(M1)***

$x = 0.0935114\ldots \times 310 + 7.43053\ldots \ (= 36.4190\ldots)$

$36$ (accept $37$ or $36.4$) ***A1***

> **Note:** Award ***(M1)A1FT*** for $x = 37$ found from using $y = 9.39x - 41.5$.  
> Award ***(M1)A0FT*** for a correct ***FT*** answer that lies outside $[15,\ 46]$.

questions.stem: The temperature of a cup of tea, $t$ minutes after it is poured, can be modelled by $H(t) = 21 + 75e^{-0.08t}$, $t \geq 0$. The temperature is measured in degrees Celsius ($^\circ$C).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(i) Find the initial temperature of the tea.

(ii) Find the temperature of the tea three minutes after it is poured.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Interpret the meaning of your answer to part (b) in the given context.
parts.markscheme:
3 valid descriptors, in any order: ***A2***

- at 3 minutes (or when $t = 3$)
- cooling/decreasing (do not accept “changing”)
- $4.72^\circ$C min$^{-1}$ (must include units) (accept approximately 5 deg/min)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
After $k$ minutes, the tea will be below $67^\circ\text{C}$ and cool enough to drink.

Find the least possible value of $k$, where $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.
parts.markscheme:
**METHOD 1**

valid attempt to solve $H(t) = 67$ (accept an inequality) ***(M1)***

eg intersection of graphs, use of logarithms.

$6.11058\ldots$ ***(A1)***

$7$ (min) ***A1***

**METHOD 2**

valid attempt to find crossover values ***(M1)***

$(6,\ 67.4087\ldots)$ and $(7,\ 63.8406\ldots)$ ***(A1)***

$7$ (min) ***A1***

parts.label: e
parts.intro: As the tea cools, $H(t)$ approaches the temperature of the room, which is constant.
parts.text: Find the temperature of the room.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find the limit of $H'(t)$ as $t$ approaches infinity.
parts.markscheme:
**METHOD 1 (working with slopes of $H$)**

valid attempt to analyse progression of slopes of $H$ ***(M1)***

$\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} H'(t) = 0$ ***A1***

**METHOD 2 (working with $H'$)**

valid attempt to use $H'$ and large values of $t$. ***(M1)***

$\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} H'(t) = 0$ ***A1***

questions.stem:
An engineer is designing a gutter to catch rainwater from the roof of a house.

The gutter will be open at the top and is made by folding a piece of sheet metal $45\text{ cm}$ wide and $600\text{ cm}$ long.

**diagram not to scale**

![A flat sheet of metal 45 wide and 600 long is folded into an open gutter with two vertical sides and a curved bottom.](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q9a.png)

The cross-section of the gutter is shaded in the following diagram.

**diagram not to scale**

![Cross-section: width w at the top, vertical sides of 10, and arc AB of a circle with centre O and radius 12; angle AOB = θ.](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q9b.png)

The height of both vertical sides is $10\text{ cm}$. The width of the gutter is $w\text{ cm}$.

Arc AB lies on the circumference of a circle with centre O and radius $12\text{ cm}$.

Let $\text{A}\hat{\text{O}}\text{B} = \theta$ radians, where $0 < \theta < \pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $\theta = 2.08$, correct to three significant figures.
parts.markscheme:
recognition that $45 = 10 + 10 +$ arc length ***(M1)***

arc length $= 25$ (cm) ***(A1)***

$25 = 12\theta$ ***A1***

$\theta = 2.08$ correct to 3 significant figures ***AG***

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the cross-section of the gutter.
parts.markscheme:
> **Note:** There are many different ways to dissect the cross-section to determine its area. In all approaches, candidates will need to find $w$ or $\dfrac{w}{2}$. Award the first three marks for work seen anywhere.

**EITHER**

evidence of using the cosine rule OR sine rule ***(M1)***

$w^2 = 12^2 + 12^2 - 2 \cdot 12 \cdot 12\cos(2.08)$ OR $\dfrac{w}{\sin(2.08)} = \dfrac{12}{\sin(0.530796\ldots)}$ ***(A1)***

$w = 20.6977\ldots$ or $\dfrac{w}{2} = 10.3488\ldots$ ***(A1)***

**OR**

using trig ratios in a right triangle with angle $\dfrac{2.08}{2}$ and side length $\dfrac{w}{2}$ ***(M1)***

$\sin\left(\dfrac{2.08}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)}{12}$ ***(A1)***

$w = 20.6977\ldots$ or $\dfrac{w}{2} = 10.3488\ldots$ ***(A1)***

> **Note:** Accept $w = 20.7179\ldots$ from use of $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{25}{24}$.

**THEN**

Let the points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H lie on the figure as follows:

![The cross-section with C and D at the top corners, G the top midpoint, E and F at the level of O on the sides, A and B at the ends of the arc and H the lowest point of the arc.](content/papers/img/2023-may-p2-tz1-q9-ms.png)

**EITHER**

(segment AHB $=$) sector OAB $-$ triangle OAB ***(M1)***

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times 2.08 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times \sin 2.08 \ (= 149.76 - 62.8655\ldots = 86.8944\ldots)$ ***(A1)***

valid approach to find total cross-sectional area (seen anywhere) ***(M1)***

sector OAB $-$ triangle OAB $+$ rectangle CDBA

$= 86.8944\ldots + 10w \ (= 86.8944\ldots + 206.977\ldots)$

> **Note:** Use of $\theta = \dfrac{25}{12}$ throughout leads to segment OAB $= 87.2517\ldots$ and cross-sectional area $= 87.2517\ldots + 207.179\ldots$.

**OR**

trapezium CGOA ($=$ rectangle CGOE $+$ triangle EOA) ***(M1)***

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \big(10 + (10 - 12\cos(1.04))\big) \times \dfrac{20.6977\ldots}{2} \ (= 72.0557)$ ***(A1)***

valid approach to find total cross-sectional area (seen anywhere) ***(M1)***

$2 \times$ trapezium CGOA $+$ sector OAB

$= 2(72.0557\ldots) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times 2.08 \ (= 144.111\ldots + 149.76)$

> **Note:** Use of $\theta = \dfrac{25}{12}$ leads to area of trapezium CGOA $= 72.2154\ldots$ and cross-sectional area $= 144.430\ldots + 150$.

**OR**

$2 \times$ area of trapezium CGOA ($=$ area of rectangle CDFE $+ 2 \times$ triangle EOA) ***(M1)***

$20.6977\ldots \times (10 - 12\cos(1.04)) + 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12\cos(1.04) \times 12\sin(1.04)$ ***(A1)***

$(= 81.2458\ldots + 62.8655\ldots)$

valid approach to find total cross-sectional area (seen anywhere) ***(M1)***

$2 \times$ trapezium CGOA $+$ sector OAB

$= 144.111\ldots + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times 2.08 \ (= 144.111\ldots + 149.76)$

> **Note:** Use of $\theta = \dfrac{25}{12}$ leads to $2 \times$ area of trapezium CGOA $= 144.430\ldots$ and cross-sectional area $= 144.430\ldots + 150$.

**THEN**

area of cross-section $= 293.871\ldots$ ($294.430\ldots$ from exact answer)

$= 294$ (cm$^2$) ***A1***

parts.label: c
parts.intro:
In a storm, the total volume, in $\text{cm}^3$, of rainwater that enters the gutter can be modelled by a function $R(t)$, where $t$ is the time, in seconds, since the start of the storm.

It was determined that the **rate** at which rainwater entered the gutter could be modelled by

$$R'(t) = 50\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{5}\right) + 3000, \ t \geq 0.$$

During any $60$-second period, if the volume of rainwater entering the gutter is greater than the volume of the gutter, it will overflow.
parts.text: Determine whether the gutter overflowed in this storm. Justify your answer.
parts.markscheme:
**METHOD 1**

volume of gutter $= 176323$ OR $176658$ (OR $600 \times$ their area) (seen anywhere) ***A1***

recognising rainfall can be represented by an integral ***(M1)***

$\displaystyle\int_0^{60} R'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \ \left(= \dfrac{250}{2\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi \times 60}{5}\right) + 3000 \times 60\right)$ ***(A1)***

> **Note:** Accept any 60 second interval or any interval which is a multiple of 5 seconds (one period) scaled up to 60 seconds e.g. $12\displaystyle\int_0^5 R'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.

rainfall over 60 seconds $= 180000$ (cm$^3$) ***A1***

the gutter will overflow because the rainfall $>$ gutter volume ***A1***

**METHOD 2**

volume of gutter $= 176323$ OR $176658$ (OR $600 \times$ their area) (seen anywhere) ***A1***

recognition that cosine has a minimum value of $-1$ ***(M1)***

$R'(t) \geq -1 \times 50 + 3000$ (cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$) ***(A1)***

rainfall over 60 seconds $\geq 177000$ ***(A1)***

the gutter will overflow because the rainfall $>$ gutter volume ***A1***

**METHOD 3**

volume of gutter $= 176323$ OR $176658$ (OR $600 \times$ their area) (seen anywhere) ***A1***

recognising rainfall can be represented by an integral ***(M1)***

attempt to solve $60 > 58.8$ OR $\displaystyle\int_0^T R'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = 176658$ ***(M1)***

time to reach overflow point $= 58.7875\ldots$ OR $58.8990\ldots$ ***A1***

the gutter will overflow because $60 > 58.8$ OR $60 > 58.9$ ***A1***
